Chapter 6: The Trap of Recognition — Why Praise and Reward Can Hold Us Back
You know, there’s a moment in almost every person’s life when the need for recognition just takes over. Think about a kid bringing home a drawing, hoping for a parent’s proud smile. Or maybe it’s you, staying late at work, quietly wishing your boss will notice. It feels like our whole world runs on praise and rewards, right? And it’s easy to start believing that recognition is the main thing fueling our growth and happiness.
But here’s something to pay attention to—underneath it all, something different is happening. The more we chase after recognition, the more we end up depending on it. That natural joy of doing, learning, or just being ourselves? It slowly gets replaced by an anxious little voice asking, “Will anyone notice?” It’s a subtle shift, but over time, it can turn even your biggest passions into just... a performance for others.
Picture a teenager who once loved playing the piano. At first, music itself was the reward—a way to express, to explore, to feel alive. But as competitions and recitals pile up, something changes. Suddenly, every note is played for the judges. Every practice session is haunted by the fear of messing up. The joy? It fades away, replaced by pressure. The piano isn’t a friend anymore—it’s a test.
That’s the trap of recognition. When praise and reward become the main goal, the activity itself starts to lose its meaning. We end up measuring our worth by how others react, and the freedom to try, to fail, to grow? It just disappears. Life becomes a stage, and every move feels like a performance.
Now, it’s not that recognition is always bad. And I’m not saying we should avoid praise altogether. But the moment these become our main motivation, they quietly chip away at confidence and creativity. Most of the time, we don’t even realize it’s happening. We just notice this growing anxiety, a fear of being overlooked, or maybe a reluctance to try new things unless we’re sure we’ll succeed.
So, what’s the alternative? It’s about finding value in the doing, not just the outcome. Playing the piano simply for the love of music. Working late because the project means something to you. Helping a friend because it feels right, not because anyone’s watching. When you shift your focus from recognition to contribution, from reward to meaning, the pressure lifts—and the joy comes back.
I’ll be honest, it’s not always easy. The world constantly tells us, “You matter if you’re noticed.” But the real truth? It’s quieter—and much deeper. Your worth isn’t something others can give or take away. It lives in the act of living, of trying, of caring, whether anyone’s watching or not.
In everyday life, this could mean celebrating effort, not just results. Trying something new, even if no one else cares. Letting go of needing to be the best, and just finding satisfaction in being true to yourself.
Over time, that need for recognition loses its grip. The world stops feeling like a stage, and starts feeling more like a playground. The courage to be disliked is, in a way, the courage to live without applause—to find meaning in the doing, not just in the praise.
